mainEntity.name: How long do dental crowns typically last before they need replacing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental crowns are designed to be long-lasting, with many lasting between 10 and 15 years or more with appropriate care. However, the lifespan of a crown depends on several factors, including the material used, the position of the tooth, oral hygiene habits, and whether the patient grinds their teeth. Regular dental check-ups allow your dental professional to monitor the condition of your crown and advise you if replacement or repair is needed. There is no fixed expiry point for a crown; clinical assessment determines when action may be appropriate.

mainEntity.name: Will teeth whitening affect my dental crown?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, standard teeth whitening treatments — including both home whitening kits and in-surgery whitening — will not alter the colour of a dental crown. Whitening agents are only effective on natural tooth enamel, not on ceramic, porcelain, or zirconia materials. If you whiten your teeth after having a crown fitted, the natural teeth may become lighter whilst the crown remains the same shade, which can create a noticeable colour mismatch. It is generally recommended to complete whitening treatment before a crown is placed, so the crown can be colour-matched to the desired result.

mainEntity.name: Why does my crown look darker near the gum?

acceptedAnswer.text: Darkening near the gum around a dental crown is a relatively common concern, particularly with older porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) crowns. The metal substructure of these crowns can cast a shadow or become visible if gum tissue recedes slightly over time, creating a dark line at the gumline. With all-ceramic crowns, darkening at the margin may occur because the natural tooth root becomes exposed as gum tissue changes with age, and root surfaces are naturally darker in colour. A dental professional can assess the cause and discuss whether any treatment is advisable.

mainEntity.name: Can I prevent my dental crown from staining?

acceptedAnswer.text: You can take practical steps to reduce the risk of staining. Using a non-abrasive toothpaste, brushing gently with a soft-bristled brush, limiting consumption of staining foods and beverages such as coffee, tea, and red wine, and avoiding tobacco products all help preserve the appearance of your crown. Attending regular dental hygiene appointments is also beneficial, as professional polishing can remove surface deposits that accumulate gradually. Wearing a nightguard if you grind your teeth can protect the glaze on porcelain crowns from premature wear.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic crown staining?

acceptedAnswer.text: Extrinsic staining refers to discolouration on the outer surface of the crown caused by external factors such as food, drink, and tobacco. This type of staining may be partially improved with professional polishing. Intrinsic discolouration refers to changes within the crown material itself — such as ageing of the ceramic or changes in the underlying tooth structure — and cannot be removed by surface cleaning. If intrinsic discolouration is causing aesthetic concern, your dental professional may discuss the option of replacing the crown with a new restoration.

mainEntity.name: Should I be concerned if my crown looks a different colour to my other teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: A noticeable colour difference between your crown and surrounding natural teeth can be frustrating, particularly if it occurs in a visible area. This may happen gradually as natural teeth change colour over time while the crown remains the same shade. It may also occur if teeth whitening treatment has been carried out after the crown was placed. This is primarily an aesthetic concern rather than a clinical emergency, but it is worth raising with your dental professional at your next check-up so that appropriate options can be discussed.
